functions.name: IRYorkAc::IRYorkAc
functions.signature: IRYorkAc::IRYorkAc(const uint16_t pin, const bool inverted = false, const bool use_modulation = true)
functions.description: Constructs a York A/C IR controller bound to a specific GPIO pin. Typical usage is to create an instance, call begin(), optionally calibrate(), configure state (mode, temp, fan, timers), then send(). The inverted and use_modulation flags control IR carrier polarity and whether to modulate the carrier (38 kHz) when transmitting.
requirements: pin must be a valid GPIO capable of IR transmission on the target platform.
If inverted is true, the IR LED drive polarity is inverted (hardware must match).
If use_modulation is false, the sender will not modulate the carrier; most IR receivers expect modulation (default true).
Call begin() before calling send().

functions.name: IRYorkAc::stateReset
functions.description: Reset the internal York protocol state to a known default. Typically restores kYorkKnownGoodState (Heat, Auto fan, Temp 24°C, Power on). Use to initialize or discard previous settings.
requirements: Caller should call calcChecksum() if it inspects or transmits the raw buffer after manual modifications; stateReset() itself is expected to produce a valid state.
Call begin() before send().

functions.name: IRYorkAc::send
functions.description: Transmit the currently configured York A/C message via IR. The message will be sent repeat+1 times as per library convention. Available only when compiled with SEND_YORK.
requirements: Must be compiled with SEND_YORK to be available.
begin() must have been called prior to the first send() to initialize the IR transmitter.
The internal state must contain a valid frame; if you changed the raw buffer, call calcChecksum() before send().
repeat is the number of extra repeats; typically 0 for a single transmission; must be a non-negative integer.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::calibrate
functions.description: Run IR carrier timing calibration for the current platform using the underlying IRsend. Produces a ~65 ms 38 kHz pulse train and returns the per-modulation timing offset to improve accuracy. Available only when compiled with SEND_YORK.
requirements: Must be compiled with SEND_YORK to be available.
Calling this will emit an IR signal; ensure it is acceptable to transmit during calibration.
Typically called at most once per object instance; cache or reuse the result if needed.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::begin
functions.description: Initialize the IR transmitter and prepare the object for use. Typically configures the GPIO and may reset or validate the internal state.
requirements: Call begin() before calling send() or calibrate().
The GPIO pin supplied to the constructor must be available and not used by other peripherals.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setPowerToggle
functions.description: Set the main unit power state flag in the York frame. Despite the name, this sets the desired power state bit (on/off) rather than issuing a literal toggle command.
requirements: on=true sets power on; on=false sets power off.
Call calcChecksum() if you will transmit after direct raw-buffer edits; setPowerToggle() itself should maintain consistency.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getPowerToggle
functions.description: Get the current power state flag from the internal York frame (1 on, 0 off).
requirements: Returns the state currently stored in the object; it does not query a physical device.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setTemp
functions.description: Set the target temperature (in °C) in the York frame.
requirements: temp must be within the supported range: kYorkMinTemp (18) to kYorkMaxTemp (32) inclusive.
Values outside the range are invalid; behavior is undefined without implementation details.
Call calcChecksum() if you modified the raw buffer manually elsewhere before sending.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getTemp
functions.description: Return the target temperature (°C) currently stored in the York frame.
requirements: Value reflects the in-memory state; it does not read from a device.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setFan
functions.description: Set the fan speed in the York frame.
requirements: speed must be one of: kYorkFanLow (1), kYorkFanMedium (2), kYorkFanHigh (3), kYorkFanAuto (8).
Other values are invalid; behavior is undefined without implementation details.
Update checksum via calcChecksum() before send() if you also edit the raw buffer directly.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getFan
functions.description: Get the fan speed currently stored in the York frame.
requirements: Returns one of the defined constants (1,2,3,8) if state is valid.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setMode
functions.description: Set the operating mode in the York frame.
requirements: mode must be one of: kYorkHeat (1), kYorkCool (2), kYorkDry (3), kYorkFan (4), kYorkAuto (8).
Other values are invalid; behavior is undefined without implementation details.
Call calcChecksum() before send() if you edited the raw buffer manually in addition to calling this.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getMode
functions.description: Get the operating mode currently stored in the York frame.
requirements: Returns one of the defined mode constants if state is valid.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getOnTimer
functions.description: Get the power-on timer value in minutes. The underlying protocol stores 10-minute units in an 8-bit field and this accessor returns minutes.
requirements: Returned value is derived from the raw 8-bit field (0–255) multiplied by 10; maximum representable is 2550 minutes if state is valid.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getOffTimer
functions.description: Get the power-off timer value in minutes. The underlying protocol stores 10-minute units in an 8-bit field and this accessor returns minutes.
requirements: Returned value is derived from the raw 8-bit field (0–255) multiplied by 10; maximum representable is 2550 minutes if state is valid.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setOnTimer
functions.description: Set the power-on timer in minutes. The value is stored in the protocol as 10-minute units in an 8-bit field.
requirements: mins must be a non-negative integer number of minutes.
The value will be quantized to 10-minute steps (i.e., stored_value = clamp(round_down(mins/10), 0..255)).
Effective representable range is 0 to 2550 minutes (0..255 in 10-minute units).
If you edited the raw buffer manually elsewhere, call calcChecksum() before sending.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setOffTimer
functions.description: Set the power-off timer in minutes. The value is stored in the protocol as 10-minute units in an 8-bit field.
requirements: mins must be a non-negative integer number of minutes.
The value will be quantized to 10-minute steps (i.e., stored_value = clamp(round_down(mins/10), 0..255)).
Effective representable range is 0 to 2550 minutes (0..255 in 10-minute units).
If you edited the raw buffer manually elsewhere, call calcChecksum() before sending.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::getRaw
functions.description: Return a pointer to the internal raw York protocol frame buffer of length kYorkStateLength. Useful for low-level inspection or modification.
requirements: The returned pointer is owned by the IRYorkAc instance; do not free it.
Length of the buffer is kYorkStateLength bytes.
After modifying the buffer contents, the caller must call calcChecksum() before sending to ensure a valid frame.
Do not use the pointer after the IRYorkAc object is destroyed.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::setRaw
functions.signature: void IRYorkAc::setRaw(const uint8_t new_code[], const uint16_t length = kYorkStateLength)
functions.description: Copy a raw York protocol frame into the object state. Allows restoring or injecting a complete frame.
requirements: new_code must be a valid, non-null pointer to at least length bytes.
length must equal kYorkStateLength for a complete York frame.
new_code is expected to contain fields matching the York format; if the checksum is not correct, caller should invoke calcChecksum() after setting or ensure provided checksum bytes are valid.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::convertMode
functions.description: Convert a common AC operating mode (stdAc::opmode_t) to the corresponding York protocol mode byte (kYorkHeat/kYorkCool/kYorkDry/kYorkFan/kYorkAuto).
requirements: Requires inclusion of stdAc type definitions (from the IRremoteESP8266 common AC abstraction).
Only standard modes that map to York are supported; unknown or unsupported inputs may map to a default or kYorkAuto depending on implementation (details not specified).

functions.name: IRYorkAc::convertFan
functions.description: Convert a common AC fan speed (stdAc::fanspeed_t) to the corresponding York protocol fan value (1 low, 2 medium, 3 high, 8 auto).

functions.name: IRYorkAc::calcChecksum
functions.description: Compute and update the 16-bit CRC-16/ARC checksum over the York frame and store it into Chk1 and Chk2. Must be called after any manual modification to the raw buffer to ensure a valid transmissible frame.
requirements: Call after any changes to the raw state (including through setRaw() if the provided checksum is unknown or incorrect).
Assumes the frame layout matches the York protocol, including the fixed checksum preamble byte (0xEC).

functions.description: Convert a York protocol mode byte to the common AC operating mode enumeration (stdAc::opmode_t).
requirements: mode should be one of the York mode constants (1 Heat, 2 Cool, 3 Dry, 4 Fan, 8 Auto).

functions.name: IRYorkAc::toCommonFanSpeed
functions.description: Convert a York protocol fan value to the common AC fan speed enumeration (stdAc::fanspeed_t).
requirements: speed should be one of the York fan constants (1 Low, 2 Medium, 3 High, 8 Auto).
Requires inclusion of stdAc type definitions.

functions.name: IRYorkAc::toCommon
functions.description: Convert the current internal York state to the library's common AC state structure (stdAc::state_t). Optionally uses a previous state as a baseline for fields not represented or not known.
requirements: Requires inclusion of stdAc type definitions.
If prev is non-null, fields not expressible in York or not set may be copied from prev; exact behavior depends on implementation.
Returned state reflects the object’s internal settings; it does not query a device.

endpoints.code:
// Build desired & prev states with arbitrary toggles to exercise resolution.
stdAc::state_t desired; stdAc::state_t prev;
int v1 = (int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % ((unsigned int)kLastDecodeType + 1));
int v2 = (int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % ((unsigned int)kLastDecodeType + 1));
IRac::initState(&desired, (decode_type_t)v1, (int16_t)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)),
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 1) != 0,
                (stdAc::opmode_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 8) - 1),
                20.0f + (float)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 150) / 10.0f,
                true,
                (stdAc::fanspeed_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 8)),
                (stdAc::swingv_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 10) - 1),
                (stdAc::swingh_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 10) - 1),
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 2) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 4) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 8) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 16) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 32) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 64) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 128) != 0,
                -1, -1);
IRac::initState(&prev, (decode_type_t)v2, (int16_t)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)),
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 1) != 0,
                (stdAc::opmode_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 8) - 1),
                20.0f + (float)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 150) / 10.0f,
                true,
                (stdAc::fanspeed_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 8)),
                (stdAc::swingv_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 10) - 1),
                (stdAc::swingh_t)((int)(*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int) % 10) - 1),
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 2) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 4) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 8) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 16) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 32) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 64) != 0,
                ((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 128) != 0,
                -1, -1);
// Randomly decide to pass prev or NULL to exercise both paths.
stdAc::state_t resolved = IRac::handleToggles(desired,
    (((*FUZZ_PARAM(unsigned int)) & 1) != 0) ? &prev : NULL);
(void)resolved.power;
// Validation: Exercise both with/without prev; no object outputs.

import random
import struct

# Data type: IR mark/space durations
# We need to provide FUZZ_PARAM_STR with bytes such that the fuzzer builds
# an even-length array of durations in microseconds (marks/spaces). The stub:
# - takes s = FUZZ_PARAM_STR()
# - selects len = 2 * pairs where pairs depends on s.size()
# - maps each byte b to v = (b % 2000); if 0 then 1. So 1..1999 usec.
# - then chooses a carrier 30k..56kHz (not influenced by our buffer)
# To exercise interesting behavior, we should:
# - Provide a non-empty string so avail_pairs > 0
# - Include varying bytes to cover small and larger durations, ensuring modulo
#   spans around boundaries (0, 1, 1999). Since 0 maps to 1, include 0x00.
# - Include values like 0x07, 0x14, etc. that after %2000 remain themselves.
# - Include values >2000 to exercise modulo wrap. Any single byte is 0..255,
#   so we cannot exceed 2000; however, repetition length selection depends on
#   s.size(), so include enough bytes (e.g., 32+) to allow up to max_pairs=8.
# - Common raw protocols: header mark (~9000), space (~4500), etc., but the
#   stub caps values to <2000. We can still create alternating patterns
#   resembling signals within the cap (e.g., 560, 560 etc.). We'll include
#   bytes that map to 560, 1690, 450, etc. Since 560 and 1690 are within 0-255?
#   No. But %2000 uses the byte directly; max 255. So we can only reach 255.
#   Hence, just provide a variety of 1..255 to create diversity.
# The function should be deterministic by seed and return <=4096 bytes.

COMMON_PATTERNS = [
    # Include zero to hit v==0 -> coerced to 1
    0x00,
    # Short pulses typical in many protocols (scaled down here)
    0x2C,  # 44
    0x38,  # 56
    0x64,  # 100
    0x78,  # 120
    0x90,  # 144
    0xA0,  # 160
    0xC8,  # 200
    0xFF,  # 255 -> 255
    # Alternating small/large-ish bytes
    0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x05, 0x08, 0x0D, 0x15,
]


def _build_sequence(rng: random.Random, min_len: int = 16, max_len: int = 64) -> bytes:
    # Ensure at least 2 bytes so avail_pairs >= 1, and enough for max_pairs=8
    # We'll build length between min_len and max_len bytes.
    n = rng.randint(min_len, max_len)
    seq = bytearray()

    # Start with a header-like burst pattern (alternating highs/lows)
    base = COMMON_PATTERNS[:]
    rng.shuffle(base)
    for b in base:
        seq.append(b)
        if len(seq) >= n:
            break

    # Fill remaining with patterned ramps and randomness to diversify modulo
    while len(seq) < n:
        mode = rng.randint(0, 3)
        if mode == 0:
            # small ramp 1..255 cycling
            start = rng.randint(1, 250)
            step = rng.randint(1, 7)
            for i in range(rng.randint(3, 7)):
                seq.append((start + i * step) & 0xFF)
                if len(seq) >= n:
                    break
        elif mode == 1:
            # bursts of a constant value
            val = rng.choice([1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 255])
            for _ in range(rng.randint(3, 10)):
                seq.append(val)
                if len(seq) >= n:
                    break
        elif mode == 2:
            # alternating small/medium values
            a = rng.choice([3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19])
            c = rng.choice([90, 120, 150, 180, 200, 220, 240])
            for _ in range(rng.randint(4, 12)):
                seq.append(a)
                if len(seq) >= n:
                    break
                seq.append(c)
                if len(seq) >= n:
                    break
        else:
            # random bytes
            for _ in range(rng.randint(4, 12)):
                seq.append(rng.randrange(0, 256))
                if len(seq) >= n:
                    break

    # Guarantee non-empty and at least 2 bytes
    if len(seq) < 2:
        seq += b"\x01\x02"
    return bytes(seq[:n])


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Choose a size targeted to allow up to 8 pairs (needs at least 16 bytes)
    # and vary to exercise different avail_pairs
    size_profile = rng.choice([
        (16, 24),   # minimal but enough for 8 pairs
        (24, 40),
        (40, 80),
        (80, 120),
    ])
    data = _build_sequence(rng, *size_profile)
    # Ensure total output <= 4096 bytes
    return data[:4096]

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Samsung A/C state bytes suitable for IRsend::sendSamsungAC(buf)
# Goal: produce a plausible Samsung AC extended (default) frame with correct section checksums
# so that decode/send paths see a valid-looking message.
#
# Samsung protocol in this library uses a fixed-length byte array (kSamsungAcStateLength).
# The extended message layout (as per SamsungProtocol::extended map) consists of 3 sections
# each with a 2-nibble (one byte split into upper/lower nibbles) checksum fields.
# Common implementations in IRremoteESP8266 store three section checksums at offsets:
#  - Section 1 checksum nibbles at bytes 1 (lower nibble) and 2 (upper nibble)
#  - Section 2 checksum nibbles at bytes 8 (lower) and 9 (upper)
#  - Section 3 checksum nibbles at bytes 15 (lower) and 16 (upper)
# And the total length commonly used for extended Samsung AC frames is 21 bytes.
#
# Checksum algorithm (per library): Sum of previous bytes in the section, then keep only low nibble
# stored as two nibbles (upper/lower) across those checksum bytes. This helper mirrors that.

DEFAULT_LEN = 21  # typical kSamsungAcExtendedStateLength

# Define simple ranges and constants for a realistic frame
MODE_VALUES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # e.g., Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan
FAN_VALUES = [0, 1, 2, 3]      # e.g., Auto, Low, Med, High
TEMP_MIN_C = 16
TEMP_MAX_C = 30


def _nibble_sum(byte_list: List[int]) -> int:
    # Return low 4 bits of sum of all bytes in the list
    return (sum(byte_list) & 0xF)


def _set_section_checksum(buf: List[int], rng, sec_start: int, sec_end_excl: int, nibl_low_index: int, nibl_high_index: int):
    # Compute checksum across bytes [sec_start, sec_end_excl) excluding the checksum placeholder bytes
    # Then place lower nibble in low-index byte lower nibble position, and upper nibble in high-index byte upper nibble.
    # For Samsung AC extended section mapping, the checksum bytes are dedicated: we store nibbles into entire bytes
    # as 0x0L at low index and 0xH0 at high index.
    # Collect all bytes except the two checksum bytes
    to_sum = []
    for i in range(sec_start, sec_end_excl):
        if i == nibl_low_index or i == nibl_high_index:
            continue
        to_sum.append(buf[i])
    nib = _nibble_sum(to_sum)
    # In the library, they often store the checksum nibble duplicated or alone; a safe approach:
    # - low checksum byte stores the lower nibble value (0x0n)
    # - high checksum byte stores the nibble in the upper position (n << 4)
    buf[nibl_low_index] = (buf[nibl_low_index] & 0xF0) | nib
    buf[nibl_high_index] = (buf[nibl_high_index] & 0x0F) | (nib << 4)


def _build_base(seed: int) -> List[int]:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    b = [0] * DEFAULT_LEN

    # Fill with a sensible baseline seen in captures: many bytes are fixed or reserved.
    # Start section 1 header bytes (0..6). We'll choose plausible constants and flags.
    # Byte 0: often a fixed intro for Samsung AC; use 0xB2 as a non-zero placeholder.
    b[0] = 0xB2
    # Bytes 1-2 will be checksum nibbles for section 1; initialize 0
    b[1] = 0x00
    b[2] = 0x00
    # Byte 3-4: filler constants
    b[3] = 0x00
    b[4] = 0x00
    # Byte 5: flags incl Sleep5, Quiet in lower bits; pick consistent zeros, maybe quiet randomly
    quiet = rng.choice([0, 1])
    sleep5 = 0
    b[5] = (sleep5 << 3) | (quiet << 2)
    # Byte 6: Power1 two-bit field in middle nibbles; 0b01 means on
    power_on = rng.choice([0, 1])
    power_bits = 0b01 if power_on else 0b00
    b[6] = power_bits << 2

    # Section 2 will start at byte 7.
    b[7] = 0x00
    # Byte 8 (checksum low nibble for section 2) and byte 9 (upper nibble + swing)
    b[8] = 0x00
    # Byte 9: lower nibble is checksum upper; upper nibble holds Swing (3 bits) + 1 reserved
    swing = rng.choice([0, 1])  # 0 off, 1 on as simple flag
    b[9] = (swing << 1)  # put swing in bit1 of upper nibble area later masked by checksum write

    # Byte 10: FanSpecial (3 bits), Display (1)
    fan_special = rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])
    display = rng.choice([0, 1])
    b[10] = (fan_special << 4) | (display << 3)

    # Byte 11: Ion and Clean toggles, Temp lower nibble
    ion = rng.choice([0, 1])
    clean = rng.choice([0, 1])
    temp_c = rng.randint(TEMP_MIN_C, TEMP_MAX_C)
    temp_field = max(0, min(15, temp_c - TEMP_MIN_C))  # map 16-30C to 0..14
    b[11] = (ion << 7) | (clean << 6) | (temp_field & 0x0F)

    # Byte 12: Fan(3), Mode(3)
    fan = rng.choice(FAN_VALUES)
    mode = rng.choice(MODE_VALUES)
    b[12] = ((fan & 0x7) << 4) | ((mode & 0x7) << 1)

    # Byte 13: BeepToggle, Power2 (2 bits)
    beep = rng.choice([0, 1])
    power2 = 0b01 if power_on else 0b00
    b[13] = (beep << 5) | (power2 << 2)

    # Section 3 bytes 14..20; many are filler and checksum
    b[14] = 0x00
    b[15] = 0x00  # checksum low nibble for section 3
    b[16] = 0x00  # checksum upper nibble for section 3
    b[17] = 0x00
    b[18] = 0x00
    b[19] = 0x00
    b[20] = 0x00

    # Now compute checksums per sections. Define section bounds:
    # Section 1: bytes 0..6 inclusive -> checksum at 1 (low), 2 (high)
    _set_section_checksum(b, rng, 0, 7, 1, 2)
    # Section 2: bytes 7..13 inclusive -> checksum at 8 (low), 9 (upper nibble)
    _set_section_checksum(b, rng, 7, 14, 8, 9)
    # Section 3: bytes 14..20 inclusive -> checksum at 15 (low), 16 (upper nibble)
    _set_section_checksum(b, rng, 14, 21, 15, 16)

    return b


def _mutate_reasonable(buf: List[int], rng):
    # Randomize a few user-facing fields within valid ranges and recompute checksums
    # Update temp, fan, mode, power, swing, flags
    temp_c = rng.randint(TEMP_MIN_C, TEMP_MAX_C)
    buf[11] = (buf[11] & 0xF0) | ((max(0, min(15, temp_c - TEMP_MIN_C))) & 0x0F)
    fan = rng.choice(FAN_VALUES)
    mode = rng.choice(MODE_VALUES)
    buf[12] = ((fan & 0x7) << 4) | ((mode & 0x7) << 1)
    # Power bits in byte 6 and 13 coherently
    p_on = rng.choice([0, 1])
    buf[6] = (buf[6] & ~0x0C) | ((0b01 if p_on else 0) << 2)
    buf[13] = (buf[13] & ~0x0C) | ((0b01 if p_on else 0) << 2)
    # Swing flag in byte 9 upper nibble area reserved bit positions
    swing = rng.choice([0, 1])
    buf[9] = (buf[9] & 0x0F) | ((swing & 1) << 4)
    # Recompute checksums
    _set_section_checksum(buf, rng, 0, 7, 1, 2)
    _set_section_checksum(buf, rng, 7, 14, 8, 9)
    _set_section_checksum(buf, rng, 14, 21, 15, 16)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    buf = _build_base(seed)
    # Add some variability across calls with same seed by additional random steps
    steps = rng.randint(0, 3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        _mutate_reasonable(buf, rng)
    # Return exactly DEFAULT_LEN bytes. The fuzzer stub mirrors this buffer across 1024 bytes.
    return bytes(buf)

from typing import List

# Generator for Sharp A/C state bytes
# The fuzzer stub calls IRsend::sendSharpAc(buf) with a 1024-byte buffer.
# Internally, Sharp AC protocol has a fixed state length kSharpAcStateLength
# (13 bytes payload with checksum nibble in the last byte as per SharpProtocol).
# We will build a valid-looking Sharp state frame of base length 13 bytes and
# then repeat it to fill the requested buffer size. We also compute the checksum
# nibble (Sum) expected by Sharp protocol: typically low 4 bits are a checksum
# over bytes 0..10/11 depending on implementation. Based on SharpProtocol
# layout provided, byte 12 contains Sum (4-bit nibble). We will compute Sum as
# the lower 4 bits of the sum of the preceding bytes' low nibbles, which matches
# many Sharp implementations.
# Fields mapping (indexes are illustrative from SharpProtocol):
#  0-3: signature/constant bytes (we choose plausible constants)
#  4: Temp (4 bits) and Model (1 bit)
#  5: PowerSpecial (upper nibble)
#  6: Mode (2), Clean (1), Fan (3)
#  7: TimerHours (4), TimerType (1), TimerEnabled (1)
#  8: Swing (3)
#  9: filler
# 10: Special
# 11: Ion (bit 2), Model2 (bit 4)
# 12: Sum (lower nibble)
# We will vary temperature, fan, mode, swing, feature flags, and timers to
# generate interesting but valid combinations, then compute the checksum nibble.

BASE_LEN = 13  # bytes in the base Sharp state we construct
OUT_LEN = 1024

# Enumerations of plausible values inferred from SharpProtocol and common AC ranges
MODES = [0, 1]  # likely Cool/Heat (2 bits)
FANS = [0, 1, 2, 3]  # 0..3 within 3 bits
TEMPS = list(range(0, 16))  # 4-bit temp field (temp offset handled by device)
SWINGS = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]  # up to 3 bits


def checksum_nibble(data: List[int]) -> int:
    # Compute 4-bit checksum nibble over bytes 0..11 (excluding checksum byte)
    # Use sum of nibbles modulo 16, similar to other Sharp-like encodings.
    total = 0
    for i in range(BASE_LEN - 1):
        b = data[i] & 0xFF
        total += (b & 0x0F) + ((b >> 4) & 0x0F)
    return total & 0x0F


def make_sharp_state(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    st = [0] * BASE_LEN

    # Bytes 0..3: choose a plausible constant header signature.
    # Not specified exactly; we keep them constant so checksum stabilizes.
    st[0] = 0xAA
    st[1] = 0x5A
    st[2] = 0xC3
    st[3] = 0x3C

    # Byte 4: Temp (4 bits) | Model (bit 4) in SharpProtocol
    temp = rng.choice(TEMPS)
    model = rng.choice([0, 1])
    st[4] = ((temp & 0x0F) | ((model & 0x01) << 4)) & 0xFF

    # Byte 5: PowerSpecial in upper nibble, lower nibble reserved
    # We can encode power on/off in high nibble patterns used by code: 0x0 for off, 0x1 for on
    power_on = rng.choice([0, 1])
    power_special = (0x1 if power_on else 0x0) << 4
    st[5] = power_special

    # Byte 6: Mode (2), Clean (1), Fan (3) packed across the byte
    mode = rng.choice(MODES) & 0x03
    clean = rng.choice([0, 1]) & 0x01
    fan = rng.choice(FANS) & 0x07
    # Pack as: [..] Mode:2 at bits 7:6, Clean at bit 5, Fan at bits 4:2
    st[6] = ((mode & 0x03) << 6) | ((clean & 0x01) << 5) | ((fan & 0x07) << 2)

    # Byte 7: TimerHours (4), TimerType (1), TimerEnabled (1)
    timer_enabled = rng.choice([0, 1])
    timer_type = rng.choice([0, 1])
    hours = rng.randrange(0, 13)  # 0..12 hours
    st[7] = ((hours & 0x0F) << 4) | ((timer_type & 0x01) << 2) | ((timer_enabled & 0x01) << 1)

    # Byte 8: Swing (3) in lower bits
    swing = rng.choice(SWINGS) & 0x07
    st[8] = swing

    # Byte 9: filler/unused
    st[9] = rng.choice([0x00, 0x10, 0x20, 0x30])

    # Byte 10: Special features (Turbo/Econo/Light toggles encoded by IRSharpAc)
    # We'll place a mix of flags; actual semantics are handled by sender.
    st[10] = rng.choice([0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x08, 0x10, 0x80])

    # Byte 11: Ion (bit 2), Model2 (bit 4)
    ion = rng.choice([0, 1])
    model2 = rng.choice([0, 1])
    st[11] = ((ion & 1) << 2) | ((model2 & 1) << 4)

    # Byte 12: Sum nibble in lower 4 bits; upper nibble can be zero
    st[12] = checksum_nibble(st)

    return bytes(st)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Create several variant Sharp frames to improve coverage, then tile to 1024 bytes.
    frames = []
    count = rng.randrange(3, 9)  # number of distinct base frames
    for _ in range(count):
        frames.append(make_sharp_state(rng))

    # Concatenate frames and repeat to reach OUT_LEN
    blob = b"".join(frames)
    if not blob:
        blob = make_sharp_state(rng)

    # Repeat to fill and then trim to 1024 bytes
    reps = (OUT_LEN + len(blob) - 1) // len(blob)
    out = (blob * reps)[:OUT_LEN]
    return out

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Sanyo A/C (standard) state bytes.
# The fuzzer stub copies our returned bytes cyclically into a 1024-byte buffer
# and calls IRsend::sendSanyoAc(buf). IR library expects a state of
# length kSanyoAcStateLength (9 bytes for standard Sanyo in this header).
# We therefore emit a short sequence that is a valid Sanyo frame, possibly
# followed by a few concatenated frames to give variety when repeated.

# Sanyo standard layout (kSanyoAcStateLength = 9):
# Byte 0: 0x6A (fixed)
# Byte 1: Temp (5 bits) -> store 16..30 C typically; library packs 5-bit value
# Byte 2: SensorTemp(5), Sensor(1), Beep(1), reserved(1)
# Byte 3: OffHour(4), reserved(4)
# Byte 4: Fan(2), OffTimer(1), reserved(1), Mode(3), reserved(1)
# Byte 5: SwingV(3), reserved(3), Power(2)
# Byte 6: reserved(3), Sleep(1), reserved(4)
# Byte 7: reserved
# Byte 8: Sum (checksum)
# Checksum algorithm per IRSanyoAc::calcChecksum(): sum of bytes 0..7 modulo 256.

# Allowed/typical ranges (heuristics based on protocol conventions):
# - Temp: 16..30 (C)
# - Mode: 0..4 (e.g., Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan; mapping internal to library)
# - Fan: 0..3
# - Power: 0=off, 1=on (encoded across 2 bits; we’ll set 0 or 1 in low bit(s))
# - SwingV: 0..5 (fit in 3 bits)
# - Sleep: 0/1
# - OffTimer: 0/1 enable, OffHour: 0..12 (fits 4 bits)
# - Sensor: 0/1 (remote vs AC), Beep: 0/1


def _checksum_sanyo(frame: List[int]) -> int:
    return sum(frame[:8]) & 0xFF


def _build_sanyo_frame(r: random.Random) -> bytes:
    b0 = 0x6A
    temp_c = r.randint(16, 30)
    # Store as 5-bit value; many implementations use (temp-16) or direct 5-bit.
    # We'll store the absolute C value masked to 5 bits; library decoders accept
    # consistent values within range.
    b1 = temp_c & 0x1F

    sensor_temp = r.randint(16, 30) & 0x1F
    sensor_loc = r.randint(0, 1)  # 0=remote, 1=AC
    beep = r.randint(0, 1)
    b2 = (sensor_temp & 0x1F) | ((sensor_loc & 0x1) << 5) | ((beep & 0x1) << 6)

    off_hours = r.choice([0, r.randint(1, 12)]) & 0x0F
    b3 = (off_hours & 0x0F) << 4  # OffHour in upper nibble per layout

    fan = r.randint(0, 3) & 0x03
    off_timer_en = 1 if off_hours != 0 else 0
    mode = r.randint(0, 4) & 0x07
    b4 = (fan & 0x03) | ((off_timer_en & 0x01) << 2) | ((mode & 0x07) << 4)

    swingv = r.randint(0, 5) & 0x07
    power_on = r.randint(0, 1)
    # Power across two bits; encode 0 or 1 in LSB, leave MSB 0.
    power_bits = (power_on & 0x01)
    b5 = ((swingv & 0x07) << 5) | (power_bits & 0x03)

    sleep = r.randint(0, 1) & 0x01
    b6 = (sleep & 0x01) << 4

    # Byte 7 reserved; some firmwares keep 0x00; use a typical fixed value.
    b7 = 0x00

    frame = [b0, b1, b2, b3, b4, b5, b6, b7, 0x00]
    frame[8] = _checksum_sanyo(frame)
    return bytes(frame)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    r = random.Random(seed)
    # Build between 1 and 4 valid frames concatenated. The stub will repeat
    # our bytes to fill 1024, so short valid sequences are fine.
    n = r.randint(1, 4)
    out = bytearray()
    for _ in range(n):
        out += _build_sanyo_frame(r)
    # Ensure total output size <= 4096
    return bytes(out[:4096])

# Generator for Sanyo A/C 88-bit state bytes (kSanyoAc88StateLength = 15)
# The fuzzer stub will copy our bytes into a 1024-byte buffer and call
# IRsend::sendSanyoAc88(const uint8_t *data, const uint16_t nbytes = kSanyoAc88StateLength, ...)
# so we should return a buffer >= 15 bytes. We'll return exactly 15 bytes,
# filled as a plausible Sanyo AC 88-bit frame.
#
# Layout reference (from headers):
# Byte 0: 0xAA (fixed preamble)
# Byte 1: 0x55 (fixed preamble)
# Byte 2: [Fan:2][..:2][Mode:3][Power:1]
# Byte 3: [Temp:5][Filter:1][SwingV:1][..:1]
# Byte 4: ClockSecs (0..59)
# Byte 5: ClockMins (0..59)
# Byte 6: ClockHrs  (0..23)
# Byte 7..9: timer-related bytes (unknown; keep 0)
# Byte 10: [..:3][Turbo:1][EnableStartTimer:1][EnableStopTimer:1][Sleep:1][..:1]
# Byte 11..13: unknown/unused per model; keep 0
# Byte 14: Sum (checksum of previous bytes per kSanyoAc88 rules)
#
# We will compute checksum as simple 8-bit sum of bytes 0..13 masked to 0xFF,
# which matches typical protocol styles used elsewhere in this codebase.

FANS = [0, 1, 2]      # plausible 3-bit fan values used (low, med, high)
MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3]  # plausible 3-bit modes (auto/cool/dry/heat)


def _checksum_sanyo_ac88(payload: List[int]) -> int:
    # Sum of bytes 0..13 modulo 256
    return sum(payload[:14]) & 0xFF


def _build_sanyo_ac88(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)

    # Choose reasonable operating state combinations that vary semantics
    power_on = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    mode = rnd.choice(MODES)
    fan = rnd.choice(FANS)
    temp_c = rnd.randint(16, 30)  # typical AC range
    swingv = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    turbo = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    sleep = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    filter_on = rnd.choice([0, 1])

    # Real-time clock
    sec = rnd.randint(0, 59)
    minute = rnd.randint(0, 59)
    hour = rnd.randint(0, 23)

    # Timers
    enable_start = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    enable_stop = rnd.choice([0, 1])

    b = [0] * 15
    b[0] = 0xAA
    b[1] = 0x55

    # Byte 2: [Fan:2][res:2][Mode:3][Power:1]
    fan2 = fan & 0x3
    mode3 = mode & 0x7
    b[2] = (fan2 << 6) | (mode3 << 1) | (power_on & 0x1)

    # Byte 3: [Temp:5][Filter:1][SwingV:1][res:1]
    temp5 = max(0, min(31, temp_c - 16))  # map 16..46C into 0..30; typical 16..30
    b[3] = (temp5 << 3) | ((filter_on & 1) << 2) | ((swingv & 1) << 1)

    # Clock
    b[4] = sec & 0x3F
    b[5] = minute & 0x3F
    b[6] = hour & 0xFF

    # Bytes 7..9 unknown, keep 0 for validity
    b[7] = 0
    b[8] = 0
    b[9] = 0

    # Byte 10: [res:3][Turbo:1][EnableStart:1][EnableStop:1][Sleep:1][res:1]
    b[10] = ((turbo & 1) << 4) | ((enable_start & 1) << 3) | ((enable_stop & 1) << 2) | ((sleep & 1) << 1)

    # Bytes 11..13: 0
    b[11] = 0
    b[12] = 0
    b[13] = 0

    # Checksum
    b[14] = _checksum_sanyo_ac88(b)

    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    # Produce a state frame of length 15. The harness repeats it to fill buffer.
    return _build_sanyo_ac88(seed)

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Sanyo A/C 152-bit state bytes
# The fuzzer stub calls IRsend::sendSanyoAc152 with a uint8_t buffer and
# default nbytes (kSanyoAc152StateLength). In IRremoteESP8266, SanyoAC152
# frames are 152 bits => 19 bytes.
# We craft a plausible 19-byte frame with reasonable fields and a trailing
# checksum byte as simple sum of previous bytes modulo 256 (common in many
# AC protocols in this codebase). While the exact Sanyo 152 checksum may
# differ, providing a consistent checksum-like value increases chances of
# being considered valid by internal helpers.

SANYO152_LEN = 19  # bytes

# Some reasonable enumerations (heuristic) for fields we place:
# We won’t rely on exact bit layouts; instead we place bytes with sensible
# patterns resembling other Sanyo layouts in this project to hit diverse paths.

MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # auto, cool, dry, heat, fan (heuristic)
FANS = [0, 1, 2, 3]       # auto, low, med, high


def _checksum_simple(data: bytes) -> int:
    # Simple modulo-256 sum of all bytes except the checksum itself
    return sum(data) & 0xFF


def _encode_bcd(val: int) -> int:
    # Encode 0..99 into packed BCD (low byte). Clip range.
    v = max(0, min(99, val))
    return ((v // 10) << 4) | (v % 10)


def _build_sanyo152_frame(r: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Construct a 19-byte frame with semi-structured layout:
    b = [0] * SANYO152_LEN

    # Byte 0: header-like constant often seen in Sanyo (0x6A used in 72-bit).
    b[0] = 0x6A

    # Byte 1: temperature (centigrade 16..30 encoded as value, or 0..31)
    temp_c = r.randint(16, 30)
    b[1] = temp_c & 0x1F

    # Byte 2: sensor temp and flags (reuse from 72-bit style)
    sensor_c = r.randint(16, 32)
    sensor_bits = (sensor_c & 0x1F)
    sensor_flag = r.choice([0, 1])  # 0 remote, 1 AC
    beep = r.choice([0, 1])
    b[2] = sensor_bits | (sensor_flag << 5) | (beep << 6)

    # Byte 3: off timer low minutes BCD (0..600 mins in tens)
    off_mins = r.choice([0, r.randint(0, 600)])
    b[3] = _encode_bcd((off_mins // 10) % 100)

    # Byte 4: Fan(2) | OffTimerEnable(1) | Mode(3)
    fan = r.choice(FANS)
    off_en = 1 if off_mins > 0 else 0
    mode = r.choice(MODES)
    b[4] = ((fan & 0x3) << 6) | ((off_en & 0x1) << 5) | ((mode & 0x7) << 2)

    # Byte 5: SwingV(3) | Power(2)
    swingv = r.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])  # some positions
    power = r.choice([0, 1])
    b[5] = ((swingv & 0x7) << 5) | ((power & 0x1) << 1)

    # Byte 6: sleep flag
    sleep = r.choice([0, 1])
    b[6] = (sleep & 0x1) << 4

    # Bytes 7..10: real-time clock and on timer (use BCD minutes since midnight)
    # Put clock minutes since midnight into two BCD bytes for variety
    minutes = r.randint(0, 1439)
    hrs = minutes // 60
    mins = minutes % 60
    b[7] = _encode_bcd(mins)
    b[8] = _encode_bcd(hrs)

    # On timer minutes since now, up to 24h
    on_mins = r.choice([0, r.randint(10, 24 * 60)])
    b[9] = _encode_bcd(on_mins // 60)  # hours BCD
    b[10] = _encode_bcd((on_mins % 60))  # mins BCD

    # Byte 11..16: Feature flags and padding
    # Toggle a few common options: iFeel/sensor update, clean, filter
    clean = r.choice([0, 1])
    filter_ = r.choice([0, 1])
    sensor_update = r.choice([0, 1])
    turbo = r.choice([0, 1])
    quiet = r.choice([0, 1])

    b[11] = (clean << 2) | (filter_ << 1) | sensor_update
    b[12] = (turbo << 7) | (quiet << 6) | r.randrange(0, 64)

    # Sensor temperature again for redundancy
    b[13] = sensor_c & 0xFF

    # More reserved/padding bytes with sensible patterns
    b[14] = 0x00
    b[15] = 0xFF
    b[16] = 0x00

    # Byte 17: another mode/fan mirror for entropy
    b[17] = ((mode & 0x7) << 5) | ((fan & 0x3) << 3) | (r.randrange(0, 8))

    # Byte 18: checksum over bytes 0..17
    chk = _checksum_simple(bytes(b[:18]))
    b[18] = chk

    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    r = random.Random(seed)
    # The fuzzer reads arbitrary-length data, mirrors into a 1024-byte buffer,
    # then IR layer will only use first kSanyoAc152StateLength bytes (19).
    # Return exactly 19 bytes of a well-formed frame to maximize validity.
    frame = _build_sanyo152_frame(r)
    # Occasionally produce multiple concatenated frames to fill more data,
    # but keep under 4096.
    if r.random() < 0.25:
        n = r.randint(2, 6)
        frames: List[bytes] = [frame] + [_build_sanyo152_frame(r) for _ in range(n - 1)]
        return b"".join(frames)
    return frame

from typing import List

# Generator for Mirage A/C state bytes (kMirageStateLength = 15 bytes)
# The fuzzer stub takes our bytes and repeats them across a 1024-byte buffer,
# then calls IRsend::sendMirage(const unsigned char data[], const uint16_t nbytes = kMirageStateLength,...)
# Hence, we only need to craft the first 15 bytes to be a valid/interesting Mirage frame.

K_MIRAGE_STATE_LENGTH = 15  # bytes

# Known structure hints from Mirage120Protocol comments:
# Byte 0: Header = 0x56
# Byte 1: Temp (Celsius minus 0x5C)
# Byte 4: Lower nibble Mode, upper bits include Fan (2 bits)
# Byte 11/12/13: BCD seconds/minutes/hours for KKG9AC1, model-dependent
# Byte 14: Sum checksum (sum of previous nibbles)
# There are two model variants with different overlays (KKG9AC1 and KKG29AC1).
# We'll generate consistent states for both families to exercise different code paths.


def _checksum_sum_of_nibbles(payload: List[int]) -> int:
    """Calculate checksum as sum of all previous nibbles modulo 256.
    The protocol notes say: Byte 14 Sum = sum of all previous nibbles.
    We'll implement nibble-sum across bytes 0..13.
    """
    total = 0
    for b in payload:
        total += (b & 0xF) + ((b >> 4) & 0xF)
    return total & 0xFF


def _bcd(v: int) -> int:
    return ((v // 10) << 4) | (v % 10)


def _clamp(v: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return lo if v < lo else hi if v > hi else v


def _make_common_core(temp_c: int, mode: int, fan: int) -> List[int]:
    # Build a generic 15-byte array initialized to zeros.
    buf = [0] * K_MIRAGE_STATE_LENGTH
    # Byte 0 header
    buf[0] = 0x56
    # Byte 1 temperature encoding: Temp = Celsius - 0x5C
    # 0x5C = 92. Common AC range 16..30C -> encoded around negatives, but library expects this form.
    temp_c = _clamp(temp_c, 16, 30)
    buf[1] = (temp_c - 0x5C) & 0xFF
    # Byte 4: fan (2 bits) in low-level mapping; lower nibble = mode.
    # Keep middle bits zero. Fan: map 0..3; Mode: 0..15 but we restrict to 0..7.
    fan &= 0x3
    mode &= 0xF
    buf[4] = ((fan & 0x3) << 6) | (mode & 0xF)
    return buf


def _build_kkg9ac1(seed_rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    # Modes to try: Cool=0, Heat=1, Dry=2, Fan=3, Recycle=4 (per comments)
    mode = seed_rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
    fan = seed_rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])
    temp_c = seed_rng.randint(16, 30)
    buf = _make_common_core(temp_c, mode, fan)
    # KKG9AC1 specific bytes
    # Byte 5: bit7..1 unknown, pack Swing/Power in 7-bit field (heuristic), keep stable
    # We'll encode Power on/off and a simple swing toggle pattern via this overlay field.
    power = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    swing_v = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    buf[5] = ((power & 1) << 6) | ((swing_v & 1) << 5)
    # Turbo, Sleep, Light flags per overlay notes (bytes 6,7,3). Use reasonable toggles.
    turbo = 1 if (mode == 0 and seed_rng.random() < 0.5) else 0  # Turbo only in Cool per notes
    sleep = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    light = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    # Byte 7: Turbo at bit3 in KKG9AC1 overlay
    buf[7] = (turbo & 1) << 3
    # Byte 6: Sleep at bit0 in KKG9AC1 overlay
    buf[6] = (sleep & 1)
    # Byte 3: Light at bit4 in KKG9AC1 overlay
    buf[3] = (light & 1) << 4
    # Clock bytes (11/12/13): set a valid time in BCD to exercise clock parsing
    secs = seed_rng.randint(0, 59)
    mins = seed_rng.randint(0, 59)
    hours = seed_rng.randint(0, 23)
    buf[11] = _bcd(secs)
    buf[12] = _bcd(mins)
    buf[13] = _bcd(hours)
    # Fill other unspecified bytes with stable constants to avoid randomness causing invalidity
    for i in range(K_MIRAGE_STATE_LENGTH):
        if i in (0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14):
            continue
        # Keep them zero; library handles defaults.
        buf[i] = 0
    # Compute checksum over bytes 0..13 (sum of nibbles)
    buf[14] = _checksum_sum_of_nibbles(buf[:14])
    return buf


def _build_kkg29ac1(seed_rng: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    # Different overlay: supports many extra flags, timers, sensor temp etc.
    mode = seed_rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
    fan = seed_rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])
    temp_c = seed_rng.randint(16, 30)
    buf = _make_common_core(temp_c, mode, fan)
    # Byte 5 contains bits: SwingH(1), SwingV(1), LightToggle(1), Power(2) in overlay
    swing_h = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    swing_v = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    light_toggle = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    power = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    b5 = 0
    b5 |= (swing_h & 1) << 7
    b5 |= (swing_v & 1) << 6
    b5 |= (light_toggle & 1) << 5
    b5 |= (power & 0x3)  # place in lowest 2 bits
    buf[5] = b5
    # Byte 6: Filter(UVC) bit1, Sleep bit3, RecycleHeat bit1 from overlay; keep plausible
    sleep = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    filt = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    recycle = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    buf[6] = ((filt & 1) << 6) | ((sleep & 1) << 3) | ((recycle & 1) << 1)
    # Byte 7: SensorTemp(6), CleanToggle(1), iFeel(1)
    sensor_temp_c = _clamp(seed_rng.randint(0, 50), 0, 63)  # 6-bit
    clean_toggle = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    i_feel = seed_rng.choice([0, 1])
    buf[7] = ((sensor_temp_c & 0x3F) << 2) | ((clean_toggle & 1) << 1) | (i_feel & 1)
    # Timers (bytes 8..11): On/Off timer hours/mins in BCD-like nibble packing per overlay
    on_hrs = seed_rng.randint(0, 23)
    on_mins = seed_rng.randint(0, 59)
    off_hrs = seed_rng.randint(0, 23)
    off_mins = seed_rng.randint(0, 59)
    buf[8] = (on_hrs & 0x1F)  # keep top bits zero
    buf[9] = (on_mins & 0x3F)
    buf[10] = (off_hrs & 0x1F)
    buf[11] = (off_mins & 0x3F)
    # Turbo bit at byte 8 bit0 in overlay; align with cool mode preference
    turbo = 1 if (mode == 0 and seed_rng.random() < 0.5) else 0
    buf[8] = (buf[8] & ~0x80) | (turbo << 7)
    # Other bytes zero
    for i in range(K_MIRAGE_STATE_LENGTH):
        if i in (0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14):
            continue
        buf[i] = buf[i] if buf[i] != 0 else 0
    buf[14] = _checksum_sum_of_nibbles(buf[:14])
    return buf


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    # Choose a variant to exercise different decode/encode paths
    variant = rnd.choice(["kkg9ac1", "kkg29ac1"])
    if variant == "kkg9ac1":
        frame = _build_kkg9ac1(rnd)
    else:
        frame = _build_kkg29ac1(rnd)
    # Ensure exact 15 bytes
    frame = frame[:K_MIRAGE_STATE_LENGTH]
    return bytes(frame)

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Mitsubishi 136-bit (17 bytes) state buffers.
# Goal: produce valid-looking frames that can exercise different code paths
# (checksums, modes, temps, fan, swing, power) while remaining within the
# protocol’s expected value ranges.

# Protocol notes (from header layout):
# Byte indices (0-based):
# 0..4   : padding/constant header bytes (often fixed in captures)
# 5      : ..... ..PP (Power in bit 1 of byte 5 in the layout; in 136 it maps
#                      to bit 6 when counting from MSB in the struct packing)
# 6      : Mode(3), -, Temp(4)   (Mode is 0..7 typical; Temp is 0..15 with an
#                                 offset used by the real device)
# 7      : -, Fan(2), -, SwingV(4)
# The library will calculate/verify checksum internally; we’ll generate sane
# values for fields and fill the rest with common constants.

# While exact fixed header bytes can vary among models, using a commonly seen
# Mitsubishi header pattern improves plausibility. We’ll start from a known-good
# seed and vary fields.

# Reasonable field ranges (typical for Mitsubishi AC protocols):
# - Mode: {0=Auto,1=Cool,2=Dry,3=Heat,4=Fan} subset within 0..7
# - Temp: device usually supports 16..31 C. Stored as (TempC - 16) in 4 bits.
# - Fan:  {0=Auto,1=Low,2=Med,3=High}
# - SwingV: 0..5 or 0..7 depending model; we keep it 0..5 plus a couple specials.
# - Power: 0/1
# The remaining bytes we fill with stable constants and simple checksum-like
# filler, but we won’t compute a real checksum as the fuzz target doesn’t require
# validity, only full length. Nevertheless, producing consistent-looking frames
# is helpful for downstream logic.

HEADER_TEMPLATE = [
    0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x00  # plausible preamble/pad bytes seen in dumps
]


def _clamp(v: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return max(lo, min(hi, v))


def _encode_mode(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # Bias toward common modes but allow exploration
    choices = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
    weights = [3, 5, 3, 5, 3, 1, 1, 1]
    return rng.choices(choices, weights=weights, k=1)[0]


def _encode_temp_c(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # Choose a Celsius temp 16..31, encode as (t-16) in 4 bits.
    t = rng.randint(16, 31)
    return t - 16


def _encode_fan(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # 0..3; bias to auto/med
    return rng.choices([0, 1, 2, 3], weights=[4, 2, 3, 2], k=1)[0]


def _encode_swingv(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # 0..5 typical, allow 6/7 occasionally
    v = rng.choices(list(range(0, 8)), weights=[4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1], k=1)[0]
    return v


def _base_frame() -> List[int]:
    # Start with 17 bytes initialized
    frame = [0x00] * 17
    # Header/pad
    frame[0:5] = HEADER_TEMPLATE
    # Put some stable filler in trailing bytes; these are often zero or small constants
    # We’ll set them after specific fields.
    return frame


def _apply_fields(frame: List[int], power: int, mode: int, temp_n: int, fan: int, swingv: int, rng: random.Random) -> None:
    # Byte 5: bits: xxxx xxP? in comments; in the union for 136, Power is the 7th bit.
    # We’ll set bit position 6 (0x40) as power, keep others stable.
    b5 = frame[5]
    b5 &= ~0x40
    if power:
        b5 |= 0x40
    frame[5] = b5

    # Byte 6: Mode (3 bits, top) and Temp (4 bits, bottom nibble) with a spacer bit
    # According to union: Mode occupies 3 high bits after one spacer; Temp low 4 bits.
    # We approximate layout: [Mode(3) << 5] | [0 spacer bit << 4] | Temp(4)
    frame[6] = ((mode & 0x7) << 5) | ((0 & 0x1) << 4) | (temp_n & 0xF)

    # Byte 7: Fan(2) in bits 6..5, SwingV(4) in low nibble
    frame[7] = ((fan & 0x3) << 5) | (swingv & 0x0F)

    # Remaining bytes: keep plausible constants/zeros
    # Bytes 8..15 often include checks/unused; we’ll place mild variability
    for i in range(8, 16):
        if frame[i] == 0:
            frame[i] = rng.choice([0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x10, 0x20, 0x00])

    # Byte 16: checksum placeholder (not computed). Use simple sum nibble to look sane.
    s = sum(frame[0:16]) & 0xFF
    frame[16] = s


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Build a diverse yet valid-looking frame
    frame = _base_frame()

    power = rng.randint(0, 1)
    mode = _encode_mode(rng)
    temp_n = _encode_temp_c(rng)
    fan = _encode_fan(rng)
    swingv = _encode_swingv(rng)

    _apply_fields(frame, power, mode, temp_n, fan, swingv, rng)

    return bytes(frame)

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Mitsubishi 112-bit A/C state bytes (14 bytes)
# Target stubs:
# - IRMitsubishi112::setRaw expects exactly 14 bytes (kMitsubishi112StateLength)
# - IRsend::sendMitsubishi112 reads from a buffer, but providing a valid 14-byte
#   state helps exercise protocol code paths.
#
# Mitsubishi112Protocol layout summary (from headers):
#   Bytes 0-4   : header/fixed/pad
#   Byte 5      : bits: [.. .. Power:1 ..] (power flag exists)
#   Byte 6      : Mode:3 (upper), others reserved
#   Byte 7      : Temp:4 (nibble, temp mapping via library)
#   Byte 8      : Fan:3, SwingV:3
#   Byte 13     : Sum (checksum over prior bytes)
# A valid-looking frame uses known header values and a correct checksum.

# Reasonable value ranges (typical for Mitsubishi 112 variant in library):
# - Mode: 0..4 (Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan)
# - Temp nibble: values map to Celsius range (e.g. 16..30 C). Library
#   interprets nibble plus base; we stick to 16..30 C as common range.
# - Fan: 0..5 (Auto + discrete speeds); we stay within 0..5
# - SwingV: 0..6 (positions/auto); use 0..6
# - Power: 0 or 1
# The library computes/verifies a checksum byte at the end; emulate the same
# simple checksum pattern used by many AC protocols in this codebase: sum of the
# previous bytes & 0xFF. For Mitsubishi112, the header uses a specific checksum
# routine internally, but a consistent 8-bit sum over bytes 0..12 matches the
# library’s expected scheme for this family.

# Known good header seed used by IRMitsubishi112 in this codebase:
# The first 5 bytes are a constant sequence for this protocol in many examples.
# We’ll use a common Mitsubishi AC header seen across variants (not critical for
# exercising code, but helps produce realistic frames):
#   0x23 0xCB 0x26 0x01 0x00
# These values are consistent with similar Mitsubishi frames; even if slightly
# variant, the object’s setRaw accepts arbitrary bytes and later code paths are
# still exercised.

_HEADER = [0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x00]

MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan
FANS = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # Auto, low..high (range seen in lib)
SWINGV = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]  # positions incl auto


def _checksum_mitsu112(payload: List[int]) -> int:
    # Simple 8-bit sum over first 13 bytes as a plausible checksum for this family.
    # If the exact protocol differs, setRaw() still takes the buffer, and this sum
    # yields a stable, reproducible byte to vary frames.
    return sum(payload[:13]) & 0xFF


def _build_frame(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    b = [0] * 14
    # Header/prefix
    b[:5] = _HEADER[:]

    # Byte 5: Power flag present at bit 5 (from union it was bit layout with Power:1 somewhere).
    # We place power as bit 5 to emulate presence. Other bits reserved 0.
    power = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[5] = (power & 0x1) << 5

    # Byte 6: Mode in top 3 bits (per union: Mode:3 then 5 reserved)
    mode = rnd.choice(MODES)
    b[6] = (mode & 0x7) << 5

    # Byte 7: Temp:4 high nibble (union shows Temp:4 then 4 reserved)
    # Map Celsius 16..30 to nibble the library expects (commonly temp-16)
    temp_c = rnd.randint(16, 30)
    temp_nibble = max(0, min(15, temp_c - 16))
    b[7] = (temp_nibble & 0xF) << 4

    # Byte 8: Fan:3 (bits 5..7), SwingV:3 (bits 2..4)
    fan = rnd.choice(FANS)
    swingv = rnd.choice(SWINGV)
    b[8] = ((fan & 0x7) << 5) | ((swingv & 0x7) << 2)

    # Bytes 9-12: leave as 0; occasionally set one to a small non-zero for variety
    if rnd.random() < 0.5:
        b[9] = rnd.randint(0, 255)
    if rnd.random() < 0.3:
        b[10] = rnd.randint(0, 255)
    if rnd.random() < 0.2:
        b[11] = rnd.randint(0, 255)
    if rnd.random() < 0.1:
        b[12] = rnd.randint(0, 255)

    # Byte 13: checksum over bytes 0..12
    b[13] = _checksum_mitsu112(b)

    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    # Produce one valid-looking 14-byte Mitsubishi112 frame.
    return _build_frame(rnd)

import random
from typing import List

def _mitsubishi_ac_state_from_fields(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Build a plausible 18-byte (144-bit) Mitsubishi AC frame matching Mitsubishi144Protocol layout hints.
    b = bytearray(18)
    # Bytes 0-4: signature/preamble seen in real captures. Use common values.
    # Many implementations start with: 0x23,0xCB,0x26,0x01,0x00 (example); use stable but varied pattern.
    sig = [0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x00]
    b[0:5] = bytes(sig)

    # Byte 5: bit5 (value 0x20) is Power. Other bits vary; set reserved bits low.
    power = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[5] = (0x20 if power else 0x00)

    # Byte 6: Mode in bits 2:0; ISee bit maybe bit2 from MS side in header, but we keep 3-bit mode.
    # Common modes mapping (not strict): 0=Auto,1=Cool,2=Dry,3=Heat,4=Fan
    mode = rnd.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) & 0x7
    b[6] = mode

    # Byte 7: Temp nibble (bits 3:0) with optional half-degree bit 4.
    # Mitsubishi often encodes Celsius as temp-16 in 4 bits (16..31C). Choose 16..30C.
    temp_c = rnd.randint(16, 30)
    temp_nibble = (temp_c - 16) & 0x0F
    half = rnd.choice([0, 1])  # 0.5 degree flag
    b[7] = temp_nibble | (0x10 if half else 0x00)

    # Byte 8: WideVane (SwingH) 4-bit field (0..7). Choose 0..7.
    wide_vane = rnd.randint(0, 7) & 0x0F
    b[8] = wide_vane

    # Byte 9: Fan (3 bits), Vane (3 bits), FanAuto (bit0/7 depending). We'll pack as: [Fan:0..5]<<5 | [Vane:0..6]<<2 | Auto
    fan_speeds = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # include Auto(0) through high variants
    fan = rnd.choice(fan_speeds) & 0x7
    vane = rnd.randint(0, 6) & 0x7
    fan_auto = 1 if fan == 0 else 0
    b[9] = ((fan & 0x7) << 5) | ((vane & 0x7) << 2) | (fan_auto & 0x1)

    # Byte 10: Clock (minutes since some epoch in 8-bit). Put plausible minutes 0..59 encoded as mins.
    b[10] = rnd.randint(0, 59)

    # Byte 11: StopClock
    b[11] = rnd.randint(0, 59)

    # Byte 12: StartClock
    b[12] = rnd.randint(0, 59)

    # Byte 13: Timer(3 bits) and WeeklyTimer(1 bit). Pack into lower nibble, upper nibble 0.
    timer = rnd.randint(0, 5) & 0x7
    weekly = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[13] = (timer & 0x7) | ((weekly & 0x1) << 3)

    # Byte 14: Ecocool bit (bit2 per struct). Place it at bit2.
    ecocool = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[14] = (ecocool & 0x1) << 2

    # Byte 15: DirectIndirect(2), AbsenseDetect(1), iSave10C(1). Put in bits 7..0 roughly; use lower nibble.
    direct_indirect = rnd.randint(0, 3)
    absense = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    isave10 = rnd.choice([0, 1]) if (mode == 3) else 0  # only meaningful in Heat
    b[15] = ((direct_indirect & 0x3) << 6) | ((absense & 0x1) << 5) | ((isave10 & 0x1) << 2)

    # Byte 16: NaturalFlow(bit6) and VaneLeft(3 bits) around mid bits; we set lower nibble as vane-left.
    natural = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    vane_left = rnd.randint(0, 6) & 0x7
    b[16] = ((natural & 0x1) << 6) | ((vane_left & 0x7) << 2)

    # Byte 17: checksum placeholder; will compute simple sum over first 17 bytes modulo 256
    csum = sum(b[0:17]) & 0xFF
    b[17] = csum

    return bytes(b)


def _random_valid_or_edge_case(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    # Generate a mix of typical and edge-case valid states to exercise different code paths
    choice = rnd.random()
    if choice < 0.4:
        return _mitsubishi_ac_state_from_fields(rnd)
    # Edge cases: toggle flags, extremes of temperature and fan
    b = bytearray(_mitsubishi_ac_state_from_fields(rnd))
    # Extreme temperatures
    if choice < 0.6:
        # Min temp
        b[7] = (0 if (b[7] & 0x10) == 0 else 0x10)
    elif choice < 0.8:
        # Max temp (30C -> nibble 14)
        b[7] = (14 & 0x0F) | (b[7] & 0x10)
    else:
        # 0.5C flag toggled
        b[7] ^= 0x10
    # Fan extremes
    fan = 0 if choice < 0.7 else 5
    vane = rnd.randint(0, 6)
    fan_auto = 1 if fan == 0 else 0
    b[9] = ((fan & 0x7) << 5) | ((vane & 0x7) << 2) | fan_auto
    # Recompute checksum
    b[17] = sum(b[0:17]) & 0xFF
    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    data = _random_valid_or_edge_case(rnd.randrange(1 << 30))
    # The fuzzer repeats the provided bytes across a 1024 buffer and also uses
    # the first 18 bytes directly. Return exactly 18 bytes.
    return data[:18]

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Mitsubishi Heavy 88-bit A/C state bytes
# Goal: Produce likely-valid frames matching the MitsubishiHeavy 88 protocol layout
# so that sender/setRaw/checksum/signature routines see realistic inputs.
#
# Protocol summary from headers (Mitsubishi88Protocol):
# - raw length: kMitsubishiHeavy88StateLength bytes (not defined here, but 11 bytes
#   are explicitly referenced in the bitfield view, so we assume >= 11). Typical
#   implementations for 88-bit is 11 bytes. We'll generate 11 bytes.
# - Fields (by byte index):
#   [0..4]  Sig (signature/fixed header)
#   [5]     bits: SwingV5(1), SwingH1(2 bits), Clean(1), others reserved
#   [6]     reserved
#   [7]     bits: SwingV7(2), Fan(3), others reserved
#   [8]     reserved
#   [9]     Mode(3), Power(1), Temp(4)
#
# Known reasonable values (heuristics):
# - Signature bytes are often fixed values. We will use a common pattern observed
#   in MHI messages for 88-bit class: 0x23,0xCB,0x26,0x01,0x00 (not guaranteed but
#   plausible). We'll also vary them across seeds while keeping a valid-looking
#   structure: first four constant-like, fifth as a simple checksum nibble.
# - Mode: 3 bits, typically: 0=Auto,1=Cool,2=Dry,3=Heat,4=Fan (library varies).
# - Power: 0 or 1.
# - Temp: 4 bits. Common encoded temp is offset from 16C. We'll map 16..30C to
#   0x0..0xE when possible.
# - Fan: 3 bits, values map to Auto/Low/Med/High.
# - Swing bits: various toggles.
# - Clean: boolean.
#
# We will construct:
#   raw[0..4] signature bytes with a plausible fixed pattern.
#   raw[5]    compose SwingH1(2), SwingV5(1), Clean(1) in documented bit spots.
#   raw[6]    zero or fixed value 0x00.
#   raw[7]    SwingV7(2), Fan(3) in spots.
#   raw[8]    zero.
#   raw[9]    Temp(4) | Power(1) | Mode(3) in documented order.
#   raw[10]   a simple checksum byte over 0..9 to mimic trailing checksum field.
#
# Note: The union in the header lists only up to byte 9 explicitly, but the state
# array length for 88-bit is 11 bytes. We'll place a checksum at byte 10. The
# library's validChecksum will likely compute its own; even if our checksum rule
# differs, data is still structurally consistent and exercises code paths.
#
# We keep total <=4096 bytes per the harness; here it's just 11.

SIG_DEFAULT = [0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x00]

MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan (plausible mapping)
FAN_VALUES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]  # 3-bit range; we prefer 0..3


def _rand_bool(r: random.Random) -> int:
    return 1 if r.random() < 0.5 else 0


def _encode_temp_c_to_nibble(temp_c: int) -> int:
    # Map 16..30C into 0..14 (4-bit), clamp within 0..15
    base = max(16, min(30, temp_c))
    return max(0, min(15, base - 16))


def _build_frame(r: random.Random) -> bytearray:
    raw = bytearray(11)
    # Signature/header bytes
    sig = SIG_DEFAULT.copy()
    # Randomly vary last signature byte to introduce diversity but keep plausible
    sig[4] = r.choice([0x00, 0xFF, 0x00, 0x10, 0x20])
    for i in range(5):
        raw[i] = sig[i]

    # Byte 5: bits layout (from union comment):
    # bit7..bit0 unknown order in doc, but we place fields as low bits to mid:
    # We'll set: SwingH1 uses 2 bits, Clean 1 bit, SwingV5 1 bit.
    swing_v5 = _rand_bool(r)
    swing_h = r.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])  # 2 bits
    clean = _rand_bool(r)
    b5 = 0
    # Place as: [ .... .... ] arbitrary mapping to low bits to avoid out-of-range
    # We'll put: b0=SwingV5, b1..b2=SwingH1, b3=Clean
    b5 |= (swing_v5 & 0x1) << 0
    b5 |= (swing_h & 0x3) << 1
    b5 |= (clean & 0x1) << 3
    raw[5] = b5

    # Byte 6: reserved, keep 0x00 or a fixed typical value
    raw[6] = r.choice([0x00, 0x20, 0x00])

    # Byte 7: SwingV7 (2 bits), Fan (3 bits)
    swing_v7 = r.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])
    fan = r.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])  # prefer standard speeds
    b7 = 0
    # Place swing_v7 in bits 4..5 per comment ("... SwingV7 :2; Fan :3;")
    # We'll assume Fan occupies low 3 bits (0..2). SwingV7 next 2 bits (3..4).
    b7 |= (fan & 0x7)
    b7 |= (swing_v7 & 0x3) << 3
    raw[7] = b7

    # Byte 8: reserved
    raw[8] = 0x00

    # Byte 9: Mode(3), Power(1), Temp(4)
    mode = r.choice(MODES)
    power = _rand_bool(r)
    temp_c = r.randint(16, 30)
    temp_n = _encode_temp_c_to_nibble(temp_c)
    b9 = 0
    # Put Temp in high nibble, Power next, Mode low 3 bits.
    # Based on the struct: uint8_t Mode:3; uint8_t Power:1; uint8_t Temp:4;
    # That implies: bits 0..2 Mode, bit3 Power, bits4..7 Temp.
    b9 |= (mode & 0x7)
    b9 |= (power & 0x1) << 3
    b9 |= (temp_n & 0xF) << 4
    raw[9] = b9

    # Byte 10: simple checksum over bytes 0..9 (8-bit sum)
    csum = sum(raw[0:10]) & 0xFF
    raw[10] = csum
    return raw


def _mutate_variants(base: bytearray, r: random.Random) -> List[bytearray]:
    variants = [base]
    # Produce a few related frames to exercise multiple code paths (e.g. power off,
    # different mode/fan). Not used by this harness directly, but kept for ease
    # of future extension.
    # Toggle power
    v = bytearray(base)
    v[9] ^= (1 << 3)
    v[10] = (sum(v[0:10]) & 0xFF)
    variants.append(v)

    # Change mode cyclically
    v2 = bytearray(base)
    mode = (v2[9] & 0x7)
    mode = (mode + 1) & 0x7
    v2[9] = (v2[9] & ~0x7) | mode
    v2[10] = (sum(v2[0:10]) & 0xFF)
    variants.append(v2)

    # Bump temp within nibble
    v3 = bytearray(base)
    temp = (v3[9] >> 4) & 0xF
    temp = (temp + 1) & 0xF
    v3[9] = (v3[9] & 0x0F) | (temp << 4)
    v3[10] = (sum(v3[0:10]) & 0xFF)
    variants.append(v3)

    return variants


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    r = random.Random(seed)
    frame = _build_frame(r)
    # Return a single frame; fuzzer will reuse it across different stubs.
    return bytes(frame)

import random
from typing import List

# Mitsubishi Heavy 152-bit A/C state bytes generator
# Goal: Produce valid-looking 152-bit (19-byte) state buffers that exercise
# IRMitsubishiHeavy152Ac and IRsend::sendMitsubishiHeavy152.
# The fuzz harness feeds our bytes to:
#  - IRsend::sendMitsubishiHeavy152(b2) where b2 is a large buffer filled by
#    repeating our seed bytes. If we return a realistic 19-byte state, repeating
#    it across the buffer keeps internal consistency for parsers that look for
#    section signatures/structure.
#  - IRMitsubishiHeavy152Ac::setRaw(data) expects at least kMitsubishiHeavy152StateLength
#    bytes; 19 bytes is the canonical length for 152 bits.
#  - IRMitsubishiHeavy152Ac::checkZmsSig/validChecksum will be more likely to
#    accept structured frames with plausible fields and a correct checksum.
#
# Based on Mitsubishi152Protocol layout in the provided header:
#   raw[0..4]  : Signature bytes (Sig[5])
#   raw[5]     : [Mode:3 | Power:1 | ? | Clean:1 | Filter:1 | ?]
#   raw[7]     : [Temp:4 | ....]
#   raw[9]     : [Fan:4 | ....]
#   raw[11]    : [ ? | Three:1 | .. | D:1 | SwingV:3]
#   raw[13]    : [SwingH:4 | ....]
#   raw[15]    : [ .... | Night:1 | Silent:1]
#   raw[17]    : checksum (Sum)
# Bytes not explicitly defined should be set to sensible defaults (often 0).
# Many implementations use fixed signature/preamble bytes; common values seen in
# open-source decoders are 0x23 0xCB 0x26 0x01 0x00 (example). We’ll generate a
# small set of plausible signatures and pick among them.
#
# Checksum: In the real implementation, checksum is typically an 8-bit sum over
# the previous bytes (sometimes modulo 256) for this family. Several MHI
# variants (88/152) use additive checksum over bytes excluding the checksum byte.
# We'll compute simple 8-bit sum of bytes 0..16 and place it at byte 17.
# This produces internally consistent frames for many decoders.

MHI152_LEN = 19  # 152 bits / 8 = 19 bytes

# Some plausible 5-byte signatures seen across MHI variants. Using a few
# options increases coverage in protocol matching.
SIG_CANDIDATES: List[bytes] = [
    bytes([0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x00]),
    bytes([0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x01, 0x20]),
    bytes([0x23, 0xCB, 0x26, 0x43, 0x00]),
]

# Enumerations with typical ranges for ACs
MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # e.g., Auto, Cool, Dry, Heat, Fan
FANS = [0, 1, 2, 3]      # Auto/Low/Med/High (packed in 4 bits)
SWINGV = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # plausible vertical positions
SWINGH = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # plausible horizontal positions
TEMPS_C = list(range(16, 31))  # 16..30°C typical


def _checksum_sum8(data: bytes) -> int:
    return sum(data) & 0xFF


def _encode_frame(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    b = bytearray(MHI152_LEN)

    # Signature
    sig = rnd.choice(SIG_CANDIDATES)
    b[0:5] = sig

    # Pick settings
    power_on = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    mode = rnd.choice(MODES) & 0x7
    fan = rnd.choice(FANS) & 0xF
    temp_c = rnd.choice(TEMPS_C)
    # Protocol stores Temp in 4 bits (likely temp-16)
    temp_nibble = max(0, min(0xF, temp_c - 16))

    swing_v = rnd.choice(SWINGV) & 0x7
    swing_h = rnd.choice(SWINGH) & 0xF
    silent = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    night = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    clean = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    filter_on = rnd.choice([0, 1])

    # Byte 5: [Mode:3 | Power:1 | ?:1 | Clean:1 | Filter:1 | ?:1]
    b5 = 0
    b5 |= (mode & 0x7) << 5
    b5 |= (power_on & 0x1) << 4
    b5 |= (clean & 0x1) << 2
    b5 |= (filter_on & 0x1) << 1
    b[5] = b5

    # Byte 6 left as 0 or minor flags; keep 0 for simplicity
    b[6] = 0

    # Byte 7: [Temp:4 | rest]
    b[7] = (temp_nibble & 0xF) << 4

    # Byte 8: WideVane (swing H encoded differently on 144-bit; for 152 we'll keep 0)
    b[8] = 0

    # Byte 9: [Fan:4 | ....]
    b[9] = (fan & 0xF)

    # Bytes 10-12 timers/clock -> zero
    b[10] = 0
    b[11] = 0
    b[12] = 0

    # Byte 11 also contains SwingV with fields Three/D; place SwingV in LS 3 bits
    # Layout hint: Byte 11: [... D:1 | SwingV:3]
    # Put D=0, Three=0, SwingV in low 3 bits
    b[11] = (swing_v & 0x7)

    # Byte 13: [SwingH:4 | ...]
    b[13] = (swing_h & 0xF) << 4

    # Byte 14: reserved
    b[14] = 0

    # Byte 15: [... | Night:1 | Silent:1]
    b15 = 0
    b15 |= (night & 0x1) << 1
    b15 |= (silent & 0x1)
    b[15] = b15

    # Byte 16: reserved
    b[16] = 0

    # Byte 17: checksum over 0..16
    b[17] = _checksum_sum8(bytes(b[0:17]))

    # Byte 18: trailing padding (often 0)
    b[18] = 0

    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)

    # Create between 1 and 4 concatenated valid frames to give the fuzzer more
    # material for repetition filling while staying protocol-consistent.
    frames = rnd.randint(1, 4)
    out = bytearray()
    for _ in range(frames):
        out += _encode_frame(rnd)

    # Ensure <= 4096 bytes
    return bytes(out[:4096])

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Fujitsu A/C state bytes
# We aim to create valid-looking Fujitsu long frames (kFujitsuAcStateLength)
# that can exercise IRsend::sendFujitsuAC and IRFujitsuAC::validChecksum.
#
# Notes (based on header descriptions and common Fujitsu layouts):
# - Long frame length used by the fuzzer is kFujitsuAcStateLength (typical 27 bytes).
# - The structure contains header bytes, an Id nibble, a command byte (short cmds
#   vs long fixed), length byte (remaining payload), protocol/version byte,
#   fields for power, C/F, temperature, mode, timer types, fan, swing, timers,
#   and a trailing checksum.
# - We will synthesize plausible frames and compute a checksum over the buffer.
#   The Fujitsu implementations generally use a simple 8-bit additive checksum
#   over all previous bytes (mod 256), but some models use nibble checks or
#   multi-section checks. For long Fujitsu frames in this project, the checksum
#   API IRFujitsuAC::validChecksum expects a specific computation. A robust
#   approach that tends to pass for many Fujitsu variants is: sum of all bytes
#   except the last, masked to 0xFF, equals the last byte.
# - We keep fields within known valid ranges (temp, mode, fan, swing, timers),
#   vary model/Id and flags to generate diverse yet plausible inputs.
# - If the exact checksum differs for some models, the frame may still be
#   considered invalid by validChecksum(), which is acceptable for fuzzing the
#   false-path as the stub calls it on both current and random buffers.
#
# To increase variety while staying under 4096 bytes, we output exactly one
# long frame per generate() call.

# Reasonable default long frame length seen commonly for Fujitsu in this codebase
DEFAULT_LONG_LEN = 27  # bytes (kFujitsuAcStateLength)

# Allowed/enumerated ranges inferred from many AC protocols
MODES = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # Auto/Cool/Heat/Dry/Fan (order may vary by model)
FANS = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  # Auto, Low..High variants depending on model
SWINGV = [0, 1, 2, 3]  # Off/positions
TEMP_C_RANGE = (16, 30)  # common Celsius range


def _checksum_sum8(buf: List[int]) -> int:
    s = sum(buf) & 0xFF
    return s


def _fujitsu_build_long(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = DEFAULT_LONG_LEN
    b = [0] * n

    # Header bytes: many Fujitsu frames start with 0x14 0x63 or 0x14 0x7F etc.
    # We'll pick from a small set of plausible headers.
    header_pairs = [(0x14, 0x63), (0x14, 0x7F), (0x14, 0x94), (0x14, 0xAE)]
    h0, h1 = rng.choice(header_pairs)
    b[0] = h0
    b[1] = h1

    # Byte 2: Id nibble within lower bits. Use 0..3 commonly observed.
    device_id = rng.randrange(0, 4)
    b[2] = (device_id & 0x03) << 2  # place in middle; upper/lower reserved

    # Bytes 3-4: often fixed or model specific. Keep as plausible constants.
    b[3] = 0x10
    b[4] = 0x00

    # Byte 5: Cmd for short codes; long codes often have a fixed value.
    # Use a common fixed like 0x20 or 0x00 depending on variants.
    b[5] = rng.choice([0x00, 0x20, 0x30])

    # Byte 6: RestLength (# of bytes after this byte). For 27 total bytes,
    # bytes after index 6 are (n - 7) = 20.
    b[6] = (n - 7) & 0xFF

    # Byte 7: Protocol/version marker. Choose plausible values.
    b[7] = rng.choice([0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x10, 0x40])

    # Byte 8: Power(1), Fahrenheit(1), Temp(6)
    power = rng.choice([0, 1])
    use_fahrenheit = 0  # keep Celsius to match our temp encoding
    temp_c = rng.randrange(TEMP_C_RANGE[0], TEMP_C_RANGE[1] + 1)
    temp_field = max(0, min(63, temp_c - 16))  # map 16.. to 0-based 6-bit
    b[8] = ((power & 1) << 0) | ((use_fahrenheit & 1) << 1) | ((temp_field & 0x3F) << 2)

    # Byte 9: Mode(3), Clean/10CHeat(1), TimerType(2)
    mode = rng.choice(MODES)
    clean10 = rng.choice([0, 1])
    timertype = rng.choice([0, 1, 2, 3])
    b[9] = ((mode & 0x7) << 0) | ((clean10 & 1) << 3) | ((timertype & 0x3) << 4)

    # Byte 10: Fan(3), Swing(2)
    fan = rng.choice(FANS)
    swing = rng.choice(SWINGV)
    b[10] = ((fan & 0x7) << 0) | ((swing & 0x3) << 3)

    # Bytes 11~13: Timers (Off/On minutes). Use small values.
    off_timer = rng.randrange(0, 12 * 60 + 1)  # up to 12h
    on_timer = rng.randrange(0, 12 * 60 + 1)
    # Encode 11 bits each, enable flags.
    b[11] = off_timer & 0xFF
    b[12] = ((off_timer >> 8) & 0x7) | (1 << 3) | (((on_timer & 0x7) << 4) & 0xF0)
    b[13] = (on_timer >> 3) & 0xFF

    # Byte 14: Filter(1) and some reserved bits. Keep filter random.
    filter_on = rng.choice([0, 1])
    b[14] = (filter_on & 1) << 4

    # Bytes 15..(n-2): Fill with plausible neutral values, but vary some feature bits.
    for i in range(15, n - 1):
        b[i] = 0x00
    # Add some typical flags in later region to exercise parser paths.
    # OutsideQuiet bit sometimes at byte 15 in some variants; toggle sparsely.
    if rng.random() < 0.3:
        b[15] |= 0x80

    # Compute checksum as sum(byte[0..n-2]) & 0xFF
    b[-1] = _checksum_sum8(b[:-1])

    return bytes(b)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Occasionally produce a second variant to add diversity: tweak mode/fan/temp
    frame = bytearray(_fujitsu_build_long(seed))
    if rng.random() < 0.4:
        # Mutate with valid ranges and recompute checksum
        temp_c = rng.randrange(TEMP_C_RANGE[0], TEMP_C_RANGE[1] + 1)
        temp_field = max(0, min(63, temp_c - 16))
        frame[8] = (frame[8] & ~0xFC) | ((temp_field & 0x3F) << 2) | (frame[8] & 0x03)
        frame[9] = (frame[9] & ~0x07) | (rng.choice(MODES) & 0x7)
        frame[10] = (frame[10] & ~0x07) | (rng.choice(FANS) & 0x7)
        frame[-1] = _checksum_sum8(list(frame[:-1]))
    return bytes(frame)

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Kelvinator A/C state (kKelvinatorStateLength bytes)
# The library expects a byte array encoding two repeated blocks with nibbled checksums.
# We construct a coherent state and compute both block checksums so it is accepted.

# Public API
# generate(seed: int) -> bytes

# Kelvinator protocol facts used here (from header comments):
# - Total length (kKelvinatorStateLength) is 16 bytes per half, repeated twice => 32 bytes.
# - Byte 0..6: payload; Byte 7: lower-nibble checksum Sum1 (sum of bytes 0..6, low nibble)
# - After a gap and header, bytes 8..14 repeat bytes 0..6; Byte 15: Sum2 = checksum of bytes 8..14
# - Bitfields: we keep within ranges and set fixed bits where known by comments.
#   We won’t model every feature; we choose consistent values.

K_LEN = 32  # 16 + 16

# Helpers to pack fields into the first block

def clamp(v, lo, hi):
    return max(lo, min(hi, v))


def build_first_block(rnd: random.Random) -> List[int]:
    b = [0] * 16
    # Byte 0: Mode(3), Power(1), BasicFan(2), SwingAuto(1), Sleep1or3(1)
    mode = rnd.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])  # generic mapping
    power = 1  # on
    basic_fan = rnd.choice([0, 1, 2])  # maps to a minimal fan encoding
    swing_auto = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    sleep13 = 0  # keep off to stay simple
    b[0] = ((mode & 0x7) << 0)  # will shift later per layout
    # According to header layout ordering (lsb-first listed top to bottom):
    # Reconstructing byte0 bit layout (from comments):
    # bits7..0: [unknown:1][SwingAuto:1][BasicFan:2][Power:1][Mode:3]
    b0 = ((mode & 0x7)) | ((power & 0x1) << 3) | ((basic_fan & 0x3) << 4) | ((swing_auto & 0x1) << 6)
    # sleep13 is the top bit; keep 0
    b[0] = b0 & 0xFF

    # Byte 1: Temp (4 bits), rest 0
    # Kelvinator common temp is typically 16..30 C; map to 0..15 nibble
    temp_c = clamp(rnd.randint(18, 28), 16, 30)
    temp_nibble = temp_c - 16
    b[1] = ((temp_nibble & 0xF) << 4)

    # Byte 2: Turbo, Light, IonFilter, XFan each 1 bit, placed in low nibble (per comments)
    turbo = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    light = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    ion = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    xfan = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[2] = ((turbo & 1) << 3) | ((light & 1) << 2) | ((ion & 1) << 1) | ((xfan & 1) << 0)

    # Byte 3: marker/end-of-command bits; keep defaults from comments: lower nibble often 0, bits[5:4]=01
    # Layout: [7:4]=0, [3:2]=01 (typically), [1:0]=01 end marker -> but to be conservative set 0x05 in low nibble
    b[3] = 0x05

    # Byte 4: SwingV (4), SwingH (1), rest 0
    swingv = rnd.choice([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
    swingh = rnd.choice([0, 1])
    b[4] = ((swingv & 0xF) << 4) | ((swingh & 0x1) << 3)

    # Byte 5..6: timer related; set to 0 when not used
    b[5] = 0
    b[6] = 0

    # Byte 7: checksum nibble of bytes 0..6 in low nibble; high nibble can be 0
    sum1 = sum(b[0:7]) & 0xFF
    b[7] = sum1 & 0x0F

    return b


def build_state(rnd: random.Random) -> bytes:
    first = build_first_block(rnd)

    # Build second block (bytes 8..15) which is a repeat of bytes 0..6, with its own checksum nibble.
    state = [0] * K_LEN
    # Copy first block into 0..7
    state[0:8] = first[:8]
    # Repeat payload into 8..14
    state[8:15] = first[0:7]
    # Byte 11 in second block (index 12..?) Per header, byte12..14 are extra state; we replicate exactly.

    # Compute Sum2 over bytes 8..14
    sum2 = sum(state[8:15]) & 0xFF
    state[15] = sum2 & 0x0F

    # Some implementations expect fixed marker bits in the two marker bytes (3 and 11)
    # Leave second block’s marker (byte 11 exact mirror of byte 3). Already mirrored via copy.

    return bytes(state)


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rnd = random.Random(seed)
    data = build_state(rnd)
    # The fuzzer copies the provided buffer cyclically across 1024 bytes.
    # Keeping it exactly K_LEN makes it align well and repeat a valid frame.
    return data

import random
from typing import List

# Generator for Daikin 280-bit (ESP) protocol raw state bytes.
# Target stubs:
# - IRsend::sendDaikin -> sendDaikin(dbuf, nbytes default=kDaikinStateLength)
# - IRDaikinESP::setRaw -> setRaw(uint8_t new_code[], length default=kDaikinStateLength)
# kDaikinStateLength for Daikin ESP protocol is 35 bytes (280 bits).
# The stubs will accept larger buffers, but they expect at least protocol-sized data.
# We construct plausible frames: three sections with internal checksums at
# bytes 7 (Sum1), 15 (Sum2), and 34 (Sum3) as per DaikinESPProtocol bit layout.
# We will fill reasonable fields (power/mode/temp/fan/swing flags etc.) and
# compute section checksums as simple 8-bit sums of each section's bytes
# prior to the checksum byte (common Daikin practice for this implementation).

DAIKIN_LEN = 35  # bytes (280-bit)

# Section boundaries (inclusive ranges in bytes) used by DaikinESP in this codebase:
# Section 1: bytes 0..6, checksum at byte 7
# Section 2: bytes 8..14, checksum at byte 15
# Section 3: bytes 16..33, checksum at byte 34


def _sum8(data: bytes) -> int:
    return sum(data) & 0xFF


def _build_daikin_frame(rnd: random.Random) -> bytearray:
    b = bytearray([0] * DAIKIN_LEN)

    # Reasonable defaults/preamble values often seen in captures.
    # We keep unspecified bytes as zeros; device code usually handles.
